body:
*The market for AI evaluation, audits, and Europe's room to act: an interview with Dinah Rabe, EMEA Lead of BABL AI*

Does Europe seize its chance as a middle power to play a significant role in the global AI market? Monika Schnitzer, Clemens Fuest, Daniel Privitera and others demand in their ["Transformative AI Strategy for Europe"](https://www.ifo.de/publikationen/2026/monographie-autorenschaft/transformative-ai-strategy-europe): Europe must become the global leader in AI assurance and shape the market. I could not agree more! And so do many large companies who deploy new products and services based on Frontier AI models. **"Users and Deployers Increasingly Expect Credible Third-Party Evidence Before Accepting Important Claims at Face Value,"** says Dinah Rabe, an independent AI evaluator with the Scale-Up BABL AI, and our [Beyond Beta](index.html) guest this week.

The opportunity for Europe to create a market in AI assurance is currently served on a silver platter: Dario Amodei's essay ["We must pace the frontier"](https://darioamodei.com/post/we-must-pace-the-frontier) has put **embedded evaluators into the limelight**. AI Evaluators, "who have employee-like access to verify safety practices and report incidents", as Amodei envisions, are one of his core proposals to prevent incidents like the OpenAI-Hugging Face agent swarm attack.

Dinah's boss [Shea Brown](https://www.linkedin.com/in/shea-brown-26050465/), a former professor at the University of Iowa, founded his startup [BABL AI](https://babl.ai/) in 2018, almost a decade ago, when algorithm audit was barely a phrase. BABL AI has just co-founded the first trade organization for AI assurance, PACT AI. It is one voice of AI safety organizations. Others are, for example, METR. METR's CEO and founder is [Beth Barnes](https://www.linkedin.com/in/elizabethmbarnes/), a former alignment researcher at OpenAI who left in 2022 and founded METR in December 2023. Others, like [Apollo Research](https://www.apolloresearch.ai/), [Fathom AI](https://fathom.org/), or [Transluce](https://transluce.org/) have also been a vocal part of the debate of the past weeks on AI safety.

With Dinah, we discuss what the current debate is missing, what AI testing and evaluating must focus on, and what Europe's chances are in this emerging field.

**Kirsten Rulf:** *You have been professionally evaluating AI systems for years now, for large corporate clients both in the US and in Europe. What is your perspective on the current debate?*

**Dinah Rabe:** There are all sorts of current discussions, some prompted by the recent "Hugging Face incident", surrounding AI agents having gone rogue. There are two points I find fascinating:

For one thing, I find it odd that it is being framed as a shocking surprise. We have known for months, if not years, that these models can display deceitful behaviour. The scale may come as a surprise, but the underlying behavior is simply a product of how these models were trained. This is not emergent behavior. These models were trained not to give up and to keep searching for solutions. Those are deliberate design decisions, not superintelligent machines that have suddenly decided to be "evil".

For another, what strikes me is how quickly people map the Hugging Face incident to their personal or business contexts. At this stage, this is an incident that could only really have happened in a very particular environment: inside the experimental setup of one of the big frontier AI labs. The idea that any AI agent could quietly burn through millions of tokens, link up with hundreds of other agents and simply "go rogue" for weeks or months is absurd. This did not just happen by accident. I understand why it causes alarm, but it takes rather particular conditions for AI agents to behave this way at all.

That said, I think it is healthy that incidents like this are pushing the debate further onto the political stage.

**Kirsten Rulf:** *Then what would be a more productive turn of the debate from your point of view?*

**Dinah Rabe:** What is largely missing from the debate is that, for example in the Hugging Face incident, the lab itself set many of the conditions that made this attack possible in the first place. Look at the details: running 1,200 agents for weeks takes an enormous amount of resources. Anyone who runs AI agents at regular scale and checks the bill for the tokens they consume would notice if those agents suddenly started working their way through thousands of euros' worth of tokens.

So, I do not think the failure was misjudging the model's capabilities. Rather, the organizational safeguards did not measure up to the model's capabilities. It is an experimental setting after all. What could have been done differently in its governance and socio-technical set-up to ensure safety? That is a far more interesting question than whether this incident has revealed a superintelligent system.

## *Should Frontier AI Labs Embed Independent Evaluators, and What Would That Look Like?*

**Kirsten Rulf:** *Almost all the Frontier AI Lab CEOs now call for independent evaluators like yourself to come on board and attest to the safety of their models. What do you think about that?*

**Dinah Rabe:** The big question right now is what it would actually mean to embed evaluators inside these labs.

In my view, there is far too much focus on capability evaluations themselves. Those are not really the missing piece. We have had capability benchmarks for a long time, and they are quite good at exposing problematic behavior such as gaming and deception. Those evaluations have consistently shown that frontier models are getting better at these behaviours.

The harder questions about embedded evaluators are these: What do they have access to? Are they truly independent from the labs they are evaluating? And what exactly are they evaluating? The answers to all of these questions are still up in the air, including in the AI assurance industry itself.

[The AI Evaluators Forum, a newly founded organization with members such as METR and Transluce, issued a statement stressing the importance of independence](https://aievaluatorforum.org/), which we as BABL AI generally support. But views differ on what "truly independent" means. For me, independence begins with funding: an evaluator should not ultimately depend financially on the organization they are supposed to scrutinize. It also requires some form of enforceability. An evaluator that can identify a serious problem but has no mechanism to compel action is independent in name only.

Then there is the question of what is actually at stake for us as the evaluators. If we do not do our job properly, what are the consequences? And if the labs do not let us do our job, are there consequences then for them? None of this is clear and what is really needed right now is a broader group of stakeholders coming together to design an AI assurance structure with real influence.

Otherwise, there is a genuine risk that a few outside evaluators are embedded in the labs as token safety measure, and that is the end of it. At worst, these embedded evaluators could even end up sharing the blame and legal liability the next time something goes wrong. If there are no consequences or full access, then calling them "independent evaluators" achieves very little.

And there is still the most fundamental question: what happens if we as evaluators do find something? That, too, is unclear and it needs ideally international rules.

**Kirsten Rulf:** *What skill profile does an AI evaluator need? What does an AI system or AI model audit look like on the ground?*

**Dinah Rabe:** One thing is certain: this is a team sport. No single person has all the necessary skills, because the work touches on so many different areas. You obviously need deeply technical people, machine learning experts who understand technical evaluations and how a model is built. However, to audit a model is not to build a model. The kind of expertise needed to push the frontier may be extremely scarce, but that is not the same as the expertise required to understand and evaluate these systems rigorously. And of course, AI itself is increasingly helping us, too. I am not worried about Europe's sovereignty when it comes to technical talent. Europe also has excellent universities with outstanding people.

But technical expertise alone is not enough. A serious evaluation or audit is built on a strong understanding of the law, the norms of society, and the broader context in which a system will operate. When we conduct risk assessments and ask whom we need to consider, we find that purely technical people sometimes struggle to put themselves in the system's context: Who might be affected by it, from the company itself to groups across society? Thinking about risk requires the most interdisciplinary group possible; otherwise you will always have a blind spot.

And for highly specific risk categories, such as biological risk, you always need dedicated subject-matter experts, too. No one person can cover all of that.

That is why, in our own risk assessments, we try to bring together as broad a group of experts and stakeholders as possible. And we encourage companies with in-house evaluation teams to do the same. The central questions are not only technical: Which risks do we need to consider? How should they be assessed? Which are genuinely high risks and deserve priority? Which can be set aside?

And once you have identified the relevant risks, the next step is to define metrics to evaluate them. But the answer is not always a quantitative technical analysis or a test. Some risks simply cannot be quantified.

## *Does AI Sovereignty Mean Increased AI Safety for Deployers?*

**Kirsten Rulf:** *The frontier AI crowd long treated compliance as a box-ticking exercise that did not really apply to them. They were the saviors, their models were at the frontier, and they were moving the world forward. Almost four years on, how do you see it?*

**Dinah Rabe:** The situation is starting to shift. We can see it because people increasingly recognize the risks and problems of the closed-source frontier model market. Many organizations that have so far relied mainly on API access to the big frontier models, or built them into their own AI systems, are worried about vendor lock-in: about the model being swapped out in the background without them noticing, as some clients report, or about prices being changed arbitrarily.

At the same time, open-weights models, where you have a degree of control over the weights and can run them yourself, keep getting better. And for a great many use cases, that might be good enough. There are certainly individual use cases where the frontier labs remain far ahead. But capability evaluations repeatedly show that open models lag closed-source models by somewhere between three and seven months. So it is worth asking whether that might be sufficient for some of your use cases. And evaluation then becomes much easier, too.

Of course, the added sovereignty and control you gain with an open-weights model comes at a price: you have to run it yourself, secure it yourself and so on. To some extent, you take on more responsibility. How much risk a company is willing to accept, and what matters most to it, is a very individual decision. And then it becomes much easier to test these systems for your own use cases.

## *What Does the AI Assurance Market Look Like?*

**Kirsten Rulf:** *Speaking of the options or challenges to evaluate models, what does the market for AI evaluators look like? Most players in the field are based in the US or the UK, yours included. Many are non-profits, or for-profit but independent. But there is nowhere near as much money in this market as in frontier AI.*

**Dinah Rabe:** The key is that AI evaluation and assurance does not require us to invent an entirely new profession from scratch. We work extensively with established audit and assurance frameworks, including standards such as ISAE 3000. Many of the fundamentals already exist: how you structure an assurance engagement, how you gather and verify evidence, how you document findings, and how you establish confidence in a claim. AI introduces new technical questions, but a lot of the underlying assurance discipline can be reused.

What is changing now is demand. Customers, regulators and citizens are asking more questions: Has anyone other than the vendor ever tested this system? In the vast majority of cases, when an AI provider says its model performs exceptionally well, is safe, or is fair, that claim still rests largely on its own evaluation. Sometimes there is rigorous internal testing behind it, but from the outside it is usually very difficult to verify. At best, some internal testing was done; otherwise it is closer to marketing.

That is really a question of market maturity. The same dynamic is now starting to reach frontier models: Are you just marking your own homework, or has someone else checked it? That is how a market takes shape: not because every company suddenly wants a formal audit, but because buyers and deployers increasingly expect credible third-party evidence before accepting important claims at face value.

The US is particularly interesting because the pressure there tends to come more from the market than from regulation. [We have just co-founded the first industry organisation around AI assurance](https://pactai.org/), with a key focus on standardisation, quality criteria and professionalisation of the field. That is an important development, because the long-term credibility of this market will depend not simply on having more evaluators, but on having clearer regulatory standards for what good evaluation actually looks like.

## *What Is the Role of AI Safety Institutes?*

**Kirsten Rulf:** *Speaking of regulation, what role should the state-backed AI safety institutes now springing up everywhere play?*

**Dinah Rabe:** It is a very welcome development in principle, but a lot depends on what they choose to focus on. I do not believe every country needs a safety institute running capability evaluations on frontier labs. We do not need ten institutions doing essentially the same thing. That would be an inefficient use of expertise and public money. But more importantly, I think it would be a missed opportunity if these institutes only focus on AI safety, because there are other dimensions that matter enormously at the national level and deserve attention.

For Germany and Europe, for example, there is the big question of how much room for manoeuvre we actually have when so much technological development is taking place in the United States and China. Perhaps I am influenced by my time in the German public sector, but I believe we have considerably more agency and capacity than we sometimes give ourselves credit for. We do not simply have to regard ourselves as exposed to whatever direction AI development takes elsewhere.

I would love to see these institutes, perhaps under a different name than "AI safety institute," focus as well on questions like: What do we want the future of AI in Germany or Europe to look like, and what will it take to get there? Which societal debates do we need to have now in order to make those choices deliberately?

Take the labour market, healthcare or schools. What role do we actually want AI to play in each of those areas? We may decide that certain uses of AI are technologically possible but nevertheless undesirable. That is precisely the point: technological possibility does not remove political and social choice.

In Europe, of course, the question is often framed at the European level. But even starting these conversations nationally would be extremely valuable, and would help make our debates increasingly well informed. A lot depends on how confident people feel discussing these issues, and on how much knowledge, or lack of it, there is in the field.

## *What Should AI Assurance Test?*

**Kirsten Rulf:** *When it comes to actual evaluation, we have established that there are enough standards and benchmarks for capabilities, and that the labs and think tanks do a fairly good job there. Where else in the lifecycle should evaluation take place, for frontier models or elsewhere?*

**Dinah Rabe:** The big difference between general-purpose frontier models and everything else, to draw a rough distinction, is context.

With a general-purpose large language model, you do not necessarily know how it will ultimately be used. That makes broad evaluations sensible: you test for general capabilities because the eventual application is still unclear.

As soon as that model is embedded in a particular system or used for a specific purpose, however, the picture changes. You know much more about the users, whether decisions are being made based on the output, the consequences of failure. That allows you to evaluate much more precisely.

The relevant questions become much more concrete. Who is using the system? Are consequential decisions being made on the basis of its outputs? Is the model operating in a process where the occasional error is tolerable, or one where it is not? What other controls sit around it? The sociotechnical context determines not only which risks matter, but also how rigorously particular parts of the system need to be evaluated.

You therefore have to look at the entire system around the model: What inputs flow into the model or system? What decisions are being made? What actions can it take, and, in agentic systems, how many steps can it take autonomously? What outputs does it produce, who receives them, and what happens next? In principle, you could evaluate every one of these points if there is a meaningful risk associated with it.

That is also where organisations can quickly become overwhelmed: Where do I even start? I could evaluate everything. This is where I think a risk-based approach, which is also central to the EU AI Act, is so important. Because resources are always limited. Look at the whole system systematically, decide which risks are most relevant and significant, and start your evaluation there. A company may have hundreds of use cases; start with the most critical ones. Start with the most consequential systems, the areas where failure could cause the greatest harm, and work outward from there.

At its core, that is what good AI assurance should look like: it is contextual and proportionate to risk.

## *European AI Sovereignty: A Pipe Dream?*

**Kirsten Rulf:** *You said Europe does not have to feel so helpless. Yet that has been the prevailing mood for the past two years: Europe has nothing except perhaps the EU AI Act, and the EU AI Office cannot build up evaluation capacity fast enough. We supposedly have nothing to counter with: no frontier model, no cloud provider, not even the infrastructure to host these systems properly. So we cannot really be sovereign. You see it differently.*

**Dinah Rabe:** I do. I think we sometimes treat sovereignty as too binary: either Europe has its own frontier model, cloud, chips and everything underneath them, or we have no sovereignty at all. The reality is more nuanced.

There are certainly areas where those dependencies matter enormously. But not every AI application requires the latest frontier model that can only be hosted in the cloud. There are countless use cases where I do not need OpenAI's or Anthropic's or Google's latest model, but rather an open-weights model I can simply run myself. Smaller models keep demonstrating this.

So the question should really be: Which dependencies are we comfortable with, and where do we consider control strategically important?

**Kirsten Rulf:** *A decision for the CEO.*

**Dinah Rabe:** Exactly. At company level, it becomes a strategic risk decision. What capability do I actually need? What am I giving up in return for it? How dependent am I willing to become on a particular model or cloud provider, and how easily could I move if that relationship changed?

The important thing is to make that decision consciously. Using the most powerful model available by default is not necessarily the same thing as making the best technological or safety choice.

And I think the same logic applies to Europe. Sovereignty should not mean trying to recreate the entire global technology stack inside our borders. It should mean identifying the areas where dependency would genuinely limit our ability to act, making sure we have alternatives there, and accepting interdependence where the risk is manageable.

## *The Role of Regulation Like the EU AI Act*

**Kirsten Rulf:** *We both have been part of the making of the EU AI Act in our time in the government, and we have already agreed earlier that it is fundamentally a sound approach. Now it is being implemented. For one, it would not even have covered some of these cases, nor would the Code of Practice. And implementation across Europe is still patchy. So what is the role of the AI Act now, and of those implementing it, from the EU AI Office to national authorities such as Germany's Federal Network Agency ("Bundesnetzagentur")?*

**Dinah Rabe:** It remains important to make explicit what our values in Europe are and what we consider important, such as fundamental rights. It will not capture every problematic case, and neither will the Code of Practice, but that does not make the framework irrelevant. It gives regulators, companies and standards bodies a common structure for thinking about what good AI governance should look like.

You can already see that influence in the amount of standardisation work now under way. CEN-CENELEC, ETSI, IEEE and others are doing very serious work in this area. Those standards will not be perfect in every detail, but without the AI Act I doubt we would have seen the same level of attention or urgency around developing them.

The real test, of course, will be implementation and enforcement, and how well that works, given that different national authorities will approach it very differently. The national authorities will determine how much of this actually reaches companies in practice. These entities need to carefully distinguish between genuine risk reduction and compliance that exists only on paper. Of course, there is a legitimate concern about burden, particularly for smaller companies. Anyone who has been through an ISO certification process knows how quickly compliance can turn into a paper battle. And documentation alone is never proof that good practice is actually happening.

To add a much more basic point: At the core, the AI Act asks companies to improve the quality of products and systems overall. Having a functioning quality-management system, carrying out a serious risk assessment, documenting how a system works and actually testing it before deployment, all of that is good for the product.

So for me, the success of the AI Act will depend on whether the institutions implementing it can operationalise its principles. If they do that well, the Act can become part of the infrastructure for more trustworthy AI in Europe.

**Kirsten Rulf:** *Creating verifiable evidence on "Our agent does not attack other systems," something along those lines.*

**Dinah Rabe:** Exactly, basic safety and quality management requirements. And it is funny: we regularly talk to people in heavily regulated sectors such as medical technology, and they laugh at how worked up everyone gets about the AI Act. In their world, the regulator can walk in unannounced on any given day and inspect everything. For them that is completely normal. They look at the AI Act and think: Well, that is just the basics.

Of course, the AI Act now affects many sectors and companies that have never been this regulated before. That is undoubtedly hard at first, and it surely costs resources. So the question is what the AI Office and national supervisory authorities can do to make sure it is handled as pragmatically as possible, for instance by accepting that a small company's quality management system will look different from that of a corporation with thousands of employees. The key question will be how much of a burden it actually becomes.

**Kirsten Rulf:** *And it is unclear whether market surveillance authorities have the expertise to really understand what companies are doing.*

**Dinah Rabe:** Yes. And once again, they are competing for the same talent everyone else wants. That will be an interesting question.

## *What Does the Day-to-Day of an AI Evaluator Look Like?*

**Kirsten Rulf:** *One final question: What does your day-to-day work as an auditor and evaluator look like?*

**Dinah Rabe:** The work varies a great deal.

Sometimes it is very much traditional assurance work: reviewing evidence, test reports, model documentation, governance processes and the claims a company is making about its system. On other days, it is much more hands-on. We might analyse data, design metrics, run evaluations, test specific behaviours or write code. So the work can range from audit and evidence review all the way through to quite technical evaluation.

What makes AI particularly interesting is that there is often no established playbook. We regularly run into questions where the system we need to test has never really been tested in that way, or in that particular context, before. Then the work becomes much more research-driven: What would a credible test actually look like? What evidence would be sufficient? How do we design an evaluation that is robust enough for us to stand behind the conclusion professionally?

That last point matters a great deal at BABL. An audit report is not just an internal research note. We have to be able to defend the opinions we give. In the worst case, if a client is challenged in court or by a regulator, we need to be able to explain exactly how we reached our conclusion, what evidence we relied on and where the limits of that conclusion are.

So a large part of the job is really about the boundaries of assurance. What can we genuinely establish? Which claims can we verify with confidence? Where is the evidence too weak? And where do we have to say: we simply cannot provide assurance on this yet?

That is what makes the work so varied. And as we evaluate new systems and contexts at BABL, we are continually testing and extending the boundaries of what credible AI assurance can cover.

**Kirsten Rulf:** *Thank you very much.*

title: “It Is Certainly a Bitter Pill, Because at the Moment We Have No Other Choice”
excerpt: The German government has signed a letter of intent with Nvidia to build open models for industrial and physical AI. Is Germany buying its way back into the AI race, or into its next platform dependency? Prof. Rainer Stark of TU Berlin, spokesperson of the Industrie 4.0 Research Advisory Board, on whether the deal is a trigger or a trap, what IPCEI AI can truly achieve, and what the ideal data-sovereign company looks like in 2030.
body:
The past two weeks have been a whirlwind: developments in tech sovereignty happen quicker than [our signals section](signals.html) can update and I have been moving back to the USA East Coast for a while to drive the next phase of this research project from there. Much to report already from this side of the Atlantic, but for that, there will be a separate post elsewhere. Just one cliffhanger picture below on how the Americans see the tech sovereignty debate:

![How the tech sovereignty debate looks from the other side of the Atlantic: a Financial Times ad in the US](ft-digital-shutdown.jpg)

As a consequence, this week's briefing, BeyondBeta #5, is once again real teamwork, with Marie finding with Prof. Rainer Stark someone who is truly at the heart of the key assumptions behind the German government's NVIDIA deal announcement. Hanna kindly drove the interview prep, and I recalled how often we have been here before, a big tech (or Big Tech?) announcement by the government, high hopes, and then...? But let us start at the beginning and then give the word to Rainer Stark.

## Is Germany Buying Its Way Back Into the AI Race, or Into Its Next Platform Dependency?

As we write, the Federal Ministries for Economic Affairs and for Research [signed a letter of intent with Nvidia](https://www.berliner-zeitung.de/article/bundesregierung-ki-kooperation-nvidia-10511192) to build specialized, open models for industrial and physical AI. Scooped first by Luisa Bomke, Felix Holtermann and their colleagues [in Handelsblatt](https://www.handelsblatt.com/politik/deutschland/kuenstliche-intelligenz-merz-schliesst-ki-pakt-mit-nvidia/100260948.html), the government is prepared to invest a three-digit million euro sum; Siemens, Audi and Black Forest Labs are among around a dozen companies set to join. [Siemens wants to turn its Erlangen plant](https://www.handelsblatt.com/unternehmen/industrie/ki-siemens-und-nvidia-planen-den-prototyp-der-autonomen-fabrik/100262775.html) into "a blueprint for autonomous factories all over the world", built on Nvidia's [Omniverse](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/omniverse/). The direction is right. But the core of German industry will run on the stack of one American company, which also gets to set the standards. And many large corporates and SME alike will find themselves faced with a choice: accept the new platform dependency or miss out on this push? Because one thing has become very clear with this deal and during Jensen Huang's entire Europe trip: the narrative that NVIDIA is purely providing the hardware and infrastructure for AI is void.

"It is certainly a bitter pill, because at the moment we have no other choice," says Rainer Stark, Head of the Department of Industrial Information Technology at TU Berlin, and our Beyond Beta guest this week. After 14 years at Ford, where he shared global responsibility for the digital development environment across five brands, he has spent almost two decades arguing that Germany must bring its industrial data "up from the basement": at TU Berlin, at Fraunhofer and today on the spokesperson team of the [Industrie 4.0 Research Advisory Board](https://en.acatech.de/project/the-research-council-industrie-4-0/) and as a vital member of acatech, a close government advisor and frequent guest in the Chancellery for years.

With Rainer Stark, we discuss whether the Nvidia pact is a trigger or a trap, what a European alternative built on open source and [IPCEI AI](https://www.bundeswirtschaftsministerium.de/Redaktion/EN/Dossier/ipcei-ai.html) could look like, and which KPIs would tell us that we are on the right track to 2030.

## The German Government's Nvidia Deal: Good News or Bitter Pill?

**Kirsten Rulf and Hanna Mrugalla:** *The German government has confirmed that it intends to invest a three-digit million euro sum in a collaboration with Nvidia to develop industrial AI in Germany. From the perspective of strategic and digital sovereignty as well as competitiveness: is this investment in your opinion good news, partly good news, or rather a signal that German industry has simply not managed to become digitally competitive on its own and does not expect to catch up anymore without a US tech leader?*

**Rainer Stark:** I would first assess it as decidedly positive news. It shows that the government is serious about tech transformation and that it is not as indifferent as it appeared until now. This deal can certainly act as a trigger for the economy as a whole, and that signal is important. It definitely pushes the German industry into the right direction: Our traditional industrial sectors, e.g. the automotive industry, which do bring a great many innovations with them, now have to become more daring on the digital front, too, rather than continue to show their hesitancy of the past. Jensen Huang made that very clear again over the weekend, noting that Germany has let too much potential slip away. For that reason, this initiative from the federal government is first and foremost very positive.

**Kirsten Rulf and Hanna Mrugalla:** *On the other hand, this deal once again means becoming dependent on an American company, like with the cloud hyperscalers or frontier AI labs, this time offering up the crown jewels of German industry. NVIDIA also effectively get to set industry standards for this new realm of physical AI with its Omniverse. Is that the bitter pill that Europe now must swallow?*

**Rainer Stark:** It is certainly a bitter pill, because it shows that at the moment, we have no other choice than to depend on yet another US tech giant in a core realm of digital value creation. So, this needs to be a wakeup call and we need to start now to develop other options for the future. The deal cannot be a one-off or one-sided step only, but it needs to spur further activities, and they will probably have to be pan-European from the outset, as with IPCEI AI. This deal must finally lead us to ask which technological capabilities and infrastructures we need independently. If we do not want or are not able to copy the full scope of Chinese and US activities along the entire tech stack, then which independent capabilities of our own do we need on a smaller scale? And how would that also increase our agility and competitiveness as a Middle Power?

We at TU Berlin are, for example, discussing all the time with corporates like Siemens and others if they really know what it means to encapsulate intelligence from Germany in AI models to derive competitive advantages in the short-term, while using a technology that we cannot handle sovereignly and independently. And how they can at least protect themselves somewhat technologically. That is certainly anything but ideal, but given how rapidly technology landscapes are developing, it is unfortunately unavoidable.

For example, our industry giants should consider whether they need to approach certain domains with open-source AI and other tech capabilities independent from US and China here in Europe. From my point of view, the Siemens strategy of a "ONE Tech Company" may not yet be fully and maturely thought through for the long haul, compared to the strategy which German industry players need and ought to put in place to survive and thrive in the rapidly evolving and sharply competitive future.

## How Do We Avoid a New Platform Dependency?

**Kirsten Rulf and Hanna Mrugalla:** *How can we prevent the situation in 2030 from being exactly the same as today? How do we avoid creating another platform dependency?*

**Rainer Stark:** We will see well-known European companies get involved in the IPCEI AI call, and open-source will play a major role there as a counterweight to the closed shop of the American style digital providers. Jointly we will tackle questions like "How can we provide entirely sovereign and encapsulated AI for our companies, wherever specific know-how is needed, on affordable hardware, so that it can be applied where value creation needs it the most?" For that, we have to come up with smarter trained models that can be conditioned and deployed differently than today's US and Chinese frontier models.

The question for us in Germany is currently whether the federal government, including through its instruments for breakthrough innovation like SprinD, will help support open-source as a serious alternative in the European sector. We have not yet seen proof of that. So far, we have heard rather ambivalent signals from the Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs; start-ups and university institutes are deliberately not funded. That irritates us a great deal, and it is not the case in other European countries.

## What Can the IPCEI AI Truly Achieve?

**Kirsten Rulf and Hanna Mrugalla:** *Everyone knows the US closed frontier AI models; they are household names. You are deeply involved in the European IPCEI for AI, which is indeed Europe's best shot to rival these models. Sometimes there is little understanding of what kind of project this is and how much is behind it. And so far, European politically motivated projects have often not brought the business success that we hoped for...*

**Rainer Stark:** The IPCEI AI will enable not only IT infrastructure for AI at scale, but also the training of special AI models for the industrial sector and for other core European sectors. The aim is to trigger and fundamentally fuel a sovereignty for Europe that is built on strength.

Of course, the ability to attract investments is what will determine its success. But our first impression is that large German companies want to invest massively in the Sovereign AI IPCEI. The AI models that emerge will not be the super-scale general AI models that keep emerging in China and the US. They will be frontier models that can be specialized for particular sectors, smaller in dose and with an entirely different kind of coding, so that the data of the industrial sector, for example from Europe, weighs more strongly in them, rather than the entire knowledge of the internet like in the current frontier models.

Specialized Industrial AI is where we in Europe should aim for unique selling points. In my view the IPCEI initiative is very well suited for that, but we must really push the pace.

:::info What Is IPCEI AI?
IPCEI AI is an [Important Project of Common European Interest for industry-specific artificial intelligence](https://www.bundeswirtschaftsministerium.de/Redaktion/EN/Dossier/ipcei-ai.html), prepared since the beginning of 2025 under the coordination of the German Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy. Its goal is a European AI ecosystem tailored to the needs of industry, covering the entire lifecycle of AI models: from data provision and open, competitive base models to highly specialized sector-specific models, AI operations and applications for companies and public administrations. In September 2026, 19 member states published a [joint manifesto](https://www.bundeswirtschaftsministerium.de/Redaktion/EN/Downloads/a/ai-manifesto.pdf?__blob=publicationFile&v=3) for the project. Based on national calls for expressions of interest, about 150 projects were preselected and brought together at a European matchmaking event in Berlin in March 2026. The national selection of projects and the submission of pre-notification documents to the European Commission were scheduled for September 2026, and selected projects may start at their own risk in the first quarter of 2027. The overall project still has to be approved by the Commission.
:::

## What Does the Ideal Data-Sovereign Company Look Like in 2030?

**Kirsten Rulf:** *For many years you and other experts have been saying that we need to unlock the potential of our industrial data in Germany and Europe: share data across industries, build common AI/ML models and common data spaces. That has also been at the heart of Germany's first-ever national data strategy in 2021, which I was responsible for when I still worked in the Federal Chancellery. Data sharing has been on the industry and political agenda for years now. I have myself contributed and co-negotiated to the EU Data Act. We heavily funded GAIA-X, Manufacturing-X, Factory-X and other initiatives, when I was still in the government, but even until today. But somehow this never seems to take off. What does the ideal data-sovereign European company look like in 2030 and how can we finally make it happen in Europe?*

**Rainer Stark:** First, this future data-sovereign company must put data at the heart of its business model and that means it must be set up and prepared to provide products and solutions for many markets, not just a single one, like automotive or manufacturing. That is a question of incentives and measurements: CFOs in their accounting and reporting must not weigh only the three classic factors of production, land, labour and capital, but in the future, they must give equal weight to the new factors that make the value of a company for its shareholders: information, data, and energy. With AI, energy and information/data have become the conditions for the other more classical factors to grow and create value. In my view, most traditional companies will have a hard time to stay at or reach a scale like their competitors in the US or China, if they do not make this transformation in their mindset. Unfortunately, I think most CEOs and CFOs in traditional companies in Europe today carry too much ballast and an outdated mindset for this turn-around. The ideal company therefore would really almost start from scratch again, as a sort of start-up.

For that transformation, we have to create first the talent and second the framework conditions. In Germany that is not happening, and the inflow of capital and the trust in this new value creation are viewed rather critically. "German Angst" sends its regards, and it puts off a great deal of capital and investment. So, we need a mindset change and a new CFO and CEO generation.

On the technology side, I believe a key question is again open-source, and how we can generate an European ecosystem there that is trusted and can scale in our traditional industries. We have to forge alliances across Europe and beyond, so that we get an ecosystem in which the players are cleverly coordinated with one another. European governments must strategically balance and support this. France offers many capabilities that we do not have to the same extent in Germany, and vice versa, and the same applies to the other countries.

## Stress Test: What If Access to US and Chinese Tech Is Cut Off Tomorrow?

**Kirsten Rulf and Hanna Mrugalla:** *Suppose that, because of US or Chinese export controls the know-how, hardware and software from Nvidia and the frontier providers were cut-off and gone tomorrow. What options would remain for German or European industry?*

**Rainer Stark:** I would assume the German government is at least smart enough to secure in this deal a certain degree of data sovereignty in Europe in return for the money it invests. So that even if we were cut off, they could still find the talent and experts in Europe to continue the work and rebuild. But you raise an important point: if we enter into this dependency, the question is how we demand that these big tech players generally behave themselves in Europe. It cannot be that they all have their European headquarters in Dublin for tax purposes. We must begin to renegotiate our relationships with them; for example, we can demand that they enable our talent here to create what tech and AI we want to establish in Europe ourselves, not lure our talent away. We must approach these sovereignty topics much more strategically: where can we still diversify? Where can we lower the risks by acting more multi-laterally with other Middle powers? And which core capabilities do we want to defend or acquire over the next four years as Europeans? I am not aware of such a Marshall Plan for Europe. We should not be so naive, and we must look at whom we can join forces with. We will not manage it in Germany alone. We need to place more value on the strategic side of tech. Anything else makes no sense.

## CEO Leadership or Political Process?

**Kirsten Rulf and Hanna Mrugalla:** *Who should take the lead here: should CEOs take the lead or is this a political process?*

**Rainer Stark:** Industry and politics appear as entirely disjointed worlds right now, but they also have things in common. I believe that at the moment there is no vision and leadership on how a sovereign industry takes shape; what it would demand from the government or from companies. In fairness, the government is currently doing its best under the given conditions. But we do not yet see whether industry is receptive to these efforts and joins them.

Currently CEOs are always saying "you as the government have to do this first so that we then can do that" in public conferences. But that does not solve the problem. Much more serious work needs to happen behind the scenes. We in academia stand ready, because we are neutral by nature. But we also notice that there is currently a stalemate, and we have to break through that. Otherwise, Europe and Germany in particular have zero chance to stay competitive.

title: “CEOs Must Become Diplomats for Their Own Causes”
excerpt: Chancellor Merz is in Japan to learn how it cut its dependence on China for critical raw materials. Henk de Hoop, CEO of SFA Oxford and a raw materials veteran with more than 30 years of industry experience, on why Europe will never mine its way to self-sufficiency, how far ahead China is in processing, and why CEOs must become diplomats for their own causes.
body:
*The German Chancellor in Japan, critical raw materials, China's head start and Europe's room to act: an interview with Henk de Hoop, CEO of SFA Oxford*

The German Chancellor is [Big in Japan this week](https://table.media/berlin/professional-briefing/947-kanzler-auf-indo-pazifik-tour-mitgliederentscheid-der-spd-berlin-keine-informationen-zu-dienstwagen), and so is our Beyond Beta briefing.

Friedrich Merz and his delegation of CEOs want to draw inspiration from Japan's strategy for reducing its dependence on China for critical raw materials. At the heart of Japan's success is the raw materials agency [JOGMEC](https://www.jogmec.go.jp/english/index.html), which uses state funds to invest in mining projects worldwide and maintains stockpiles. JOGMEC is often envied in Europe, German industry would like to see a similar model for Germany. An initiative led by carmaker BMW plans to present its concept for a joint raw materials trading house in November, reports [Politico](https://www.politico.eu/newsletter/berlin-playbook/berlin-tokio-kanzler-und-vizekanzler-maximal-auf-abstand/).

Absolutely the right move, says our guest this week, Henk de Hoop, CEO of SFA Oxford, the globally leading analytics company for critical raw materials, and himself a critical raw materials veteran with 30+ years of industry experience. Politicians alone cannot help here: "Some companies are already shut out of the supply chain for these metals or dual-use components, because China has put its foot down. (...) As a CEO struggling with a risky supply chain, you must become a lot more geopolitically savvy and engaged. You must push this much higher up on the government agenda. Talk to your industry peers and the broader supply chain. (...) CEOs must become diplomats for their own causes."

However, Henk de Hoop and other experts also observe that German DAX companies and other European players are still feeling their way around this topic as relative greenhorns. A dangerous phase, he warns: "Lots of money has been burned in the mining industry, even by very reputable big companies like Rio Tinto, BHP and Anglo American. They all carry scars from billion-dollar losses because, despite all the work and professionalism involved, they overlooked X, Y or Z, and it proved extremely costly. So, it is not investing for sissies."

So what can European CEOs do? Recycling is not as effective an answer to the problem as the [EU Commission and its Critical Raw Materials Act](briefings/this-is-not-investing-for-sissies.html) would like it to be. "Substitution, looking for alternative metals in your products, and reducing your dependency, is absolutely critical. However, you often find that alternatives do not deliver the same performance, efficiency or energy usage. (...) So heavy investment into R&D, now especially turbocharged using AI, is definitely a must."

How can Europe tackle the critical raw materials crisis, and are politics and industry in sync? Here is the full interview.

**Kirsten Rulf:** *In Europe, in the past few months alone, there have been a lot of developments around access to Critical Raw Materials. We see rapid implementation of key projects of the Critical Raw Materials Act and Ursula von der Leyen even mentioned the founding of a new corporation on Critical Raw Materials in her State of the Union speech. At the same time, there is now a lot of talk about mining our own critical raw materials. You have decades of experience in mining, mining finance, and now analysis. How would you evaluate the idea to start mining in the EU?*

**Henk de Hoop:** I find that there is a lot of naivety and ignorance in Europe about what it actually takes to build a profitable mine, and about the timelines and investment involved in such projects. To begin with, finding a mine is probably the hardest part. There are a lot of elements on the periodic table that would on paper be available in Europe but will never be economical to mine here. If I drop a probe into the soil next door here today, I will find lots of metals, also rare earths, but none of them in economic quantities. That is often misjudged by reading just the headlines in Europe. Geology is geology. Economically mineable deposits are scarce, geology bound, and hardly ever in locations where you want them to be. Hence, we have to go out to places like South America or the Congo to secure our copper for example.

On a positive note, what I do see now is that the politicians have at least started talking to Canada, Australia, Japan and other allies. Saudi Arabia is also currently doing a massive search campaign, going through all their old data, retesting some of their old samples, and finding critical raw material. So, there are still plenty of opportunities for the EU to find allies with prospective geology out there.

That is exactly what is needed: a combination of forces. Because we will never become self-sufficient in Europe when it comes to all of the metals considered critical or strategic.

**Kirsten Rulf:** *Just as a thought experiment, what would it need to build a viable mine here, and how long would it take?*

**Henk de Hoop:** First, you start off searching on a very wide grid, and there is a lot of geological work beforehand: field mapping, aeromagnetic surveys, analyzing historical data etc.

Many projects already drop out as a possibility along that way. You might start with 10 possible projects in the campaign, and at stage two of the assessment, seven already fall away. With the remaining three, you then go into more detail and find: oops, there is actually far less useful metal than expected. Or the geological distribution is so poor that mining will not be economical. Or there are contaminants that will result in very poor recovery or result in an unsellable concentrate. So, at every next stage of study or fine tuning promising projects fall away. But many politicians assume that once you have found some metal in the ground, you will automatically start a mine eventually down the line. If you started a proper focused geological campaign in Europe today, starting with a first stage filtering process, up to an actual feasibility study, it would probably take at least ten to twelve years to get there. So, this is not a matter of "let us set a policy and provide money and, hoppa, we have got a mine up and running in 5 years".

**Kirsten Rulf:** *And once you have a positive feasibility study, what comes next?*

**Henk de Hoop:** Then come all the engineering studies, which cover not only the mining side but also the processing route of the interesting minerals to actually retrieve them out of the soil or rock. That often means a lot of laboratory work, which also takes time. Because what you want to know very early on is whether you can recover that metal at a high enough yield and with the right quality. And you need to know what comes out as waste: Am I allowed to deposit this toxic waste close to the mine, under what conditions, and will it remain stable in the long term? It is a very expensive and multi-year testing and optimization exercise.

**Kirsten Rulf:** *Let us say a European mine is finally producing. Does that solve the supply chain problem for European companies?*

**Henk de Hoop:** No, because a mine only gets you a concentrate of these metals, and a concentrate is only the start. Next, you need to process it, for example in a specialized smelter, and every metal follows a different route to eventually refined metal or metal salts. Take copper: there might be a smelter in Bulgaria, but it may not be able to treat the concentrate from the just discovered European copper mine because of the by-products it contains. Copper smelters are not all alike. So, even if you have the mine in Europe, you may need to send the copper concentrate somewhere else outside of Europe for refining. But until you have done all the studies, you cannot predict whether your concentrate can be treated in Europe at all. And then there is the question of demand: you would have to be exceptionally lucky to find the metals, in the right mix, of the right quality, and in the right volumes to match or nearly match European demand.

**Kirsten Rulf:** *Why would there not be demand for that European metal?*

**Henk de Hoop:** Take rare earth mining for example. The economics of rare earth mining can be rather scary: a deposit might produce say six elements, some of them worthless but still needing to be disposed of one way or another, or sometimes it contains radioactive by-products. Rare earths in particular are difficult to process and upgrade, given the often dozens of complex chemical processing steps to concentrate and purify the individual elements. Eventually producing the metal in Europe does not mean anyone will buy it simply because it is "sovereign metal". Companies mostly care about the cheapest price. At SFA Oxford, we have done some work on the achievability of a green premium for lithium for example. A lot of mining companies believe: if we produce our lithium green, we will get more money for it. That has proved so far to be wishful thinking. Nobody is prepared to pay extra for green metal yet, unless regulation forces your hand and you absolutely cannot sell your end product without that green material in it.

## Why Are DAX Companies Investing in Rare Earth Mines?

**Kirsten Rulf:** *Nevertheless, I saw a lot of names investing in mines that surprised me. Schaeffler, BMW and others are big in the market, also BASF for chemicals. Why are these companies getting involved and how do you see that market for European companies that are not traditional mining companies?*

**Henk de Hoop:** These companies started about five to eight years ago to help finance new projects in certain regions without Chinese influence to get these new mining projects off the ground quicker. I think companies like BMW and General Motors are still feeling their way around the mining industry. Sure, they can help fund a rare earth mine. But first of all, these companies do not invest in greenfield projects where hardly any geological work has been done. So, they probably would not finance projects in Europe. They go for projects that are already a couple of years further along, or that have had a lot of the scientific work done already. Projects, for example, that have at least a feasibility study done.

Financing new projects is risky, because the track record of start-up mining projects is very mixed. In my time as a banker, I had lots of mining companies pitching projects to me, and there are at least 200 reasons why a banker will say no. Lots of money has been burned in the mining industry, even by very reputable big companies like Rio Tinto, BHP and Anglo American. They all carry scars from billion-dollar losses because, despite all the work and professionalism involved, they overlooked X, Y or Z, and it proved extremely costly. So, it is not investing for sissies.

Plus, the problem for BMW, Schaeffler and others is that this financing of mines still does not give them an end product and it does not make them more sovereign or less dependent on China.

The good news is that they have all woken up. This is not a two-year solution, but over the last three years it has become a real CEO-level topic. We at SFA Oxford have had far more calls than ever before around sourcing of scarce metals, now also from the defense industry. That is partly because China has taken some very tough steps on exports of niche metals. BMW and General Motors are probably only too aware of that: if tough, restrictive decisions are made, they will have a problem very quickly. Within perhaps 6 to 12 months, their production is on hold.

**Kirsten Rulf:** *Which brings us to the fact that China not only controls the critical raw material mining industry, but, almost more importantly, 95% of the processing industry that turns rare earth into magnets and other products that the automotive, defense, and energy industry needs.*

**Henk de Hoop:** That is the reality. Much of the control will remain with China, simply because it keeps on growing the downstream processing industry. Europe is trying to break in, but gaining any ground in such a fast-growing market is not easy. And China has 30 years of optimization on us, particularly in the technology in the middle of the processing chain, as the West allowed the skills and capacity to shift in decades past. China now has a huge head start. It also knows there is a threat out there and it wants to continue to dominate. So, China has been stopping any processing technology from crossing its borders. They are basically saying: "We are no longer selling these lithium upgrade machines or this refinery technology. And forget about rare earth refining technology!"

And even if Europe manages to gain some ground, in magnet manufacturing for example, there are some 40 different grades of magnet alloys out there, each with its own market. Which one do you bet on? Where are you going to focus? Again, China has spent years optimizing these grades of magnets, because it had so many clients and such diverse players in that space. Even if you get one, two or even six magnet producers up and running in Europe: Can they be economically viable? Have they got enough customers in Europe? Will they cover 80% of European demand across magnet qualities, given the enormous variety of grades? Or will they just scratch the surface, at 15% of what is needed? In that case, you have not solved your problem.

I would not call it an entirely lost race in rare earth processing, but starting from behind, we have to be realistic: Europe is not going to fully catch up.

**Kirsten Rulf:** *Besides magnets, many other technologies depend on these materials as well, chips, for example...*

**Henk de Hoop:** In general, we underestimate how complex our modern products are. Some of them need 30 or 40 different critical raw materials. So even if you as the CEO have secured supply for five of them, you still cannot build the product, if element number six or seven is blocked by a market actor or unavailable for other reasons. I can understand why CEOs and others, like R&D professionals, talk about this topic so much: there are so many angles to the supply chain problem, and so many reasons why and where the supply chain can break. Everybody in the large European companies must be aware of the need to solve this problem. But I think there is still little understanding of what is required and how company leaders could act.

## Substitution and Recycling: What Is the Way Towards More Sovereignty?

**Kirsten Rulf:** *What, from your perspective, could they do? There is a lot of talk about recycling and substitution, for example with the synthetic tetrataenite and other lab-made substitutes. Could recycling and substitution be the way out?*

**Henk de Hoop:** It must be a combination of those things. Substitution, looking for alternative metals in your products, and reducing your dependency, is absolutely critical. However, you often find that alternatives do not deliver the same performance, efficiency or energy usage. But sometimes that is the price you have to pay, rather than producing nothing at all because you cannot access the metal you need. So heavy investment into R&D, now especially turbocharged using AI, is definitely a must.

Recycling is another part of the answer. But some people in Europe, let us call them the green thinkers, believe recycling can solve everything. Not in a growing economy. Very few metals can be recycled endlessly without losing either quality or volume through yield losses. Recycling has its benefits, but the continued need for new material should not be underestimated or wished away.

What is very important for CEOs and policymakers alike, I think, is to be strategic about sharing the necessary skills and cooperating in the "lottery" of geology. And that is exactly what is happening, at a certain pace: Europe is linking up with Canada, Australia, Japan, Taiwan, Africa, South America politically. CEOs must become diplomats for their own causes, too. Take Canada for example. It has cheap power. And now that America has said it does not want Canadian aluminum anymore, Canada would happily produce cheap, abundant aluminum and send it to Europe. So, as a CEO look at the broad range of partners who can help you: Who has the strongest comparative advantage in producing a particular good? What can you offer them?

And in a way Europe is benefiting from the current US way of doing business that is not necessarily helping it make friends around the world.

**Kirsten Rulf:** *What can Europe and European CEOs offer these key partners?*

**Henk de Hoop:** That is something that European politicians and CEOs have to consider carefully. Talent would be a good option. But we need to consciously work on that. Let me start with some background. When I finished studying in 1992, there were 85 students in my year at Delft University. Probably 80 or 90 percent went into oil and gas, and only 5 of the 85 ended up in mining engineering. And this diminishing talent flow into extractive industries has become worse over time. The perception in Europe was: mining is not for us anymore, we do not need it. Mining was almost an ignored industry. Of course, the mining industry has always been there, and it is massive outside of Europe. But if you shut down an industry for 40 or 50 years, not only is much of the original knowledge gone, more importantly, you have also missed 40 years of progress. How things were done in 1980 is very different from how they are done in 2026. A lot of research elsewhere outside of Europe has gone into optimization, fine-tuning, digital know-how and IP.

A lot of that knowledge now sits in China, in the US, to a certain extent, but also in Canada, South America and Australia, the big mining regions that have stayed close to the industry and have the educational institutions to stay up to date. Without the latest talent and innovation, we will always be on the back foot. Many new companies around the world are looking at new processes and trying to catch up, because that knowledge is very much locked up in China.

That is why it is so important for Europe to connect with them. I lived in South Africa for 30 years, and there is a surplus of engineers there, because some of its mining sectors are shrinking. Australia, by contrast, is growing quite fast, and projects in Canada, South America and Africa are getting off the ground, so a real skills shortage is already developing. If Europe wants to build a knowledge center, it probably must tap into some of those talent pools first, or into people coming out of those industries in Australia or elsewhere who perhaps are willing to go back to Europe. And then build from there, to have the skills and have a bargaining chip in the future.

## What Should a CEO Do as a Next Step?

**Kirsten Rulf:** *As a last question: If you were the CEO of a defense company and fully dependent on rare earths: How would you tackle that entire value chain of mining, refining, recycling? And what else would you be thinking about?*

**Henk de Hoop:** We have already had inquiries from CEOs on this question following the last so-called blacklist that China issued, where they named a range of companies, including European defense companies, that will no longer be supplied with critical metals. So, this is not a theoretical scenario, some companies are already shut out of the supply chain for these metals or dual-use components, because China has put its foot down. Unfortunately, there is no quick fix. But one next step is now crystal clear: as a CEO struggling with a risky supply chain, you must become a lot more geopolitically savvy and engaged. You must push this much higher up on the government agenda. Talk to your industry peers and the broader supply chain. If you had asked that question as a CEO five or eight years ago, you probably would not have found any support or even a listening ear for the topic, not from your shareholders, not from the government, not from your suppliers, who would have said: "Do not worry, we will always get these materials to you." That is very different now. Today, your shareholders understand that it is a critical risk to your company's survival. The government understands it is a critical risk to the nation's defense, and that it risks losing the company to perhaps foreign direct investment or foreign regulation from a non-friendly power, if it does not help secure supply.

There is no way any one company or even an industry alliance can solve this alone. It needs strong partnership with governments and the entire supply chain.
